newsitem.title: UK: UK bank dealing profits dimmed by Natwest.
newsitem.headline: UK bank dealing profits dimmed by Natwest.

text.p: Dealing profits of British banks were sluggish in 1996 with the only bright spark -- a 12 percent jump at NatWest Markets -- dimmed by the subsequent discovery of a 50 million pound ($80.6 million) hole in its options trading.

Taking into account the NatWest gap, caused by the mispricing of options deals, UBS Phillips and Drew analyst John Aitken said he believed bank dealing profits were down about five to 10 percent across the board.

Overall pre-tax profits at NatWest Markets, the investment banking arm of National Westminster Bank Plc jumped to 462 million pounds in 1996 from 304 million in 1995. For dealing alone its profits surged 12 percent to 543 million pounds in 1996.
But this robust performance was tarnished after the bank revealed, only two days after publication of the 1996 results, the gap in its options-trading book.

The bank said a senior trader had been suspended for "failure" to supervise, pending the conclusion of an internal inquiry. A second trader, who had resigned from the bank before the errors surfaced, has been reported to Britain's banking regulator.
"The 50 million-pound hole will knock off that (dealing profits) side of it. But otherwise, their dealing profits were up quite strongly," said Ian Poulter, banking analyst at Williams de Broe.

With NatWest dealing profits dented, poor dealing results for Britain's banks were highlighted by a 45 percent slump in profits at Lloyd's TSB Group Plc to 96 million pounds before expenses from 175 million in 1995.

Standard Chartered Plc's dealing profits slid 27 million pounds to 213 million in 1996, while HSBC Holdings Plc, one of the world's largest banking groups, posted dealing profits of 515 million pounds in 1996, down from 533 million in 1995.
Dealing results at BZW, Barclays Plc investment arm, however, rose to 397 million pounds in 1996 from 388 million in 1995.
"Generally, dealing profits are in a downtrend because of lower, more stable, interest rates," Aitken said.
He, and others, also blamed the decline on a drop in volatility on Europe's foreign exchange markets and the rise of electronic broking systems, which have reduced the margins on trades.
"The foreign exchange business performed poorly in an increasingly competitive market," Barclays said in a statement accompanying full-year results.

Analysts and banking executives say it is not surprising that banks are losing their competitive edge as volatility is squeezed out of markets in the run-up to European economic and monetary union (EMU).
"Currencies are relatively stable. There is a move to converge European economies," said Aitken.
Again, NatWest's foreign exchange performance was better than most with profits steady at 176 million pounds in 1996 despite what the bank said were difficult market conditions.

"The principle difficulty was that the currency markets were not volatile and it is very difficult to make money when the foreign exchange is not volatile," said NatWest Markets chief executive Martin Owen.
But hefty dealing profits are not necessarily great news, said analysts, because that part of the banking business was unlikely to be sustainable.
"In terms of growth, one prefers to see fees and commissions looking stronger than dealing because that is the area which is probably going to be more sustainable," said de Broe's Poulter.
In 1995, for instance, dealing profits as a proportion of British bank revenues were pared to just 5.6 percent from 8.3 percent in 1993.
"The proportions are rather more comfortable than they were in 1993. And I am not looking for them to grow much greater," he said.
"I am keener to see net fees and commissions growing strong rather than running-up dealing profits by overtaking more risks," he added.
